newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn rejects SPD comment govt to fail to meet EMU.
newsitem.headline: Bonn rejects SPD comment govt to fail to meet EMU.

text.p: German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel on Monday rejected an assertion by a top opposition Social Democrat (SPD), Gerhard Schroeder, that Bonn cannot qualify for European monetary union (EMU) without "creative bookkeeping."
Bonn would not require a softening of the EMU deficit and debt criteria to quality for the single currency, Kinkel said in a statement.

"The federal government stands without exception behind its intent to introduce the euro on January 1, 1999," Kinkel said. "It is clear: There will not be a soft Euro. The strict observance of the criteria, as agreed in the (EMU) treaty, prescribes the timetable -- without creative bookkeeping."
The SPD's Gerhard Schroeder, state premier of Lower Saxony, said in an interview with the Financial Times that EMU should be delayed and that Germany would not qualify without financial trickery.

European Union members must have government budget deficits of less than three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and total debt of less than 60 percent of GDP in 1997 to qualify for the single currency launch in 1999.
Kinkel said Schroeder's comments were "irresponsible," could stir up fear among Germans and suggested Bonn was taking EMU criteria lightly. "This kind of talk I reject most sharply," he said.
Schroeder's comments were followed by a statement from Oskar Lafontaine, head of the SPD, who said on Monday the government knows it cannot meet the Maastricht deficit rule with its current policies.
This view is shared by most economic research institutes and is obvious from government budget developments, Lafontaine said.
Lafontaine said the three-percent rule was not decisive for the SPD, since Germany could demonstrate a high degree of stability on the inflation, interest rate, and currency value guidelines.
He called for a stronger emphasis on jobs-creation policies at the European level.
